Piapara (Megaleporinus obtusidens) is a medium-bodied anostomid characiform native to the Paraná-Paraguay basin, where it supports important artisanal fisheries. Maximum recorded body length in adults from large river systems approaches 76 centimeters [Li = 76 centimeters], a size attained after several years of sustained growth in productive floodplain habitats. Reproductively active females typically exhibit a substantial body mass associated with their advanced maturity, with the largest gravid specimens weighing up to 7,300 grams [Wwi = up to 7,300 grams]. This asymptotic wet weight reflects the species' capacity for considerable somatic expansion in nutrient-rich environments such as the Pantanal wetlands, where seasonal flooding provides abundant food resources. In contrast, the initial wet weight at hatching is extremely modest, with newly emerged yolk-sac larvae weighing approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams], a value consistent with the small adhesive eggs characteristic of anostomid species.

Sexual maturation in Megaleporinus obtusidens occurs at a relatively modest body size compared to its ultimate dimensions. Field surveys indicate that the onset of gonadal activity is reached at a total length of 21.6 centimeters [Lp = 21.6 centimeters], which corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of roughly 149 grams [Wwp = roughly 149 grams]. This relationship between length and mass at maturity follows the species' overall length-weight power law, whereby individuals must accumulate sufficient condition before investing in gametogenesis. The transition to reproductive status typically coincides with the second or third year of life, depending on local thermal and hydrological regimes. In the lower Paraná River, where growing seasons are prolonged, young-of-the-year can occasionally achieve pubertal dimensions within their first eighteen months, although such accelerated maturation is uncommon and likely contingent upon exceptional prey availability and warm water temperatures.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of subtropical floodplain lakes (24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C]), the species displays a maximum daily reproductive rate of approximately 10,137 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 10,137 eggs per day]. This high-frequency iteroparous strategy allows the species to exploit the protracted flood pulse, releasing multiple batches of fertilised ova over the course of the wet season. The daily reproductive rate derived from this fecundity underscores the substantial gametic investment that gravid females sustain annually. Such a reproductive schedule is energetically demanding and requires efficient food assimilation and lipid storage during the preceding dry season when feeding conditions are less predictable.

Larval development proceeds rapidly following eclosion, as the tiny yolk-sac larvae quickly absorb their endogenous reserves and initiate exogenous feeding. The transition from lecithotrophic to exotrophic nutrition is facilitated by the early development of a functional mouth gape, allowing first feeding on microcrustaceans and rotifers within a few days post-hatching. The pelagic larval phase is brief, with juveniles settling into marginal vegetated habitats once they reach approximately 2 centimeters in length. Growth during this early period is highly temperature-dependent; under the thermal regime described earlier (24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C]), the maximum longevity observed in this species reaches around 5,110 days [am = around 5,110 days], equivalent to roughly 14 years of life under captive conditions. This lifespan places Megaleporinus obtusidens among the longer-lived members of the Anostomidae, a pattern likely linked to its low natural mortality rate in environments with abundant refuge cover and moderate predation pressure from large piscivorous fishes like Pseudoplatystoma species.

Longitudinal studies of tagged individuals in the upper Paraná floodplain have provided valuable demographic data on this species. The oldest wild-caught Piapara on record was estimated to be 14 years [am = 14 years] of age, a longevity attained under the relatively stable thermal conditions of the region (24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C]). Such extended lifespans are notable among Neotropical characiforms of comparable body size and are likely facilitated by the species' omnivorous feeding habits and the seasonal availability of fruits, seeds, and aquatic invertebrates. Senescence in older females is manifested by a gradual decline in relative fecundity and egg quality, although individuals remain reproductively active well into their second decade. The combination of moderate body size, delayed maturity, high fecundity, and prolonged reproductive lifespan positions Megaleporinus obtusidens as a K-selected strategist within its trophic guild, making it particularly vulnerable to overfishing of large, fecund individuals.
